newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala said protecting human rights violators.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala said protecting human rights violators.

text.p: There were fewer human rights violations in Guatemala last year but the government failed to investigate and punish violators, a human rights organisation said on Wednesday in its annual report.
"There is no longer an institutionalized state policy to violate human rights, however the violators themselves are protected by the state," the Mutual Support Group (GAM) said.

According to its report, police and prosecutors have not investigated soldiers who have operated with apparent impunity in kidnappings, car thefts and drug crimes. During 36 years of civil war, which ended Dec. 29 with a peace treaty between the government and leftist rebels, the Guatemalan army was accused of killing and abducting tens of thousands of civilians in an attempt to wipe out support for the opposition.
GAM director Mario Polanco told Reuters the army, notorious for being untouchable by the courts, was still potentially dangerous despite changes that have brought it under civilian control.

"Despite the peace signing we believe that (army intelligence units) could at any time begin operating against any person who works with the political opposition or grassroots movements," Polanco said.

The support group's 1996 report listed 276 acts of political violence including 69 extrajudicial executions and 97 attempted killings. It based its numbers on direct reports by citizens, newspaper and police reports and the group's own independent investigations, Polanco said.
The organisation looked into the circumstances of the crimes and the occupations of the victims to decide whether the motive was political, economic or otherwise, he said.

Formed by families of disappeared people, the GAM began working 13 years ago at the height of an army reign of terror in Guatemala. The group estimates more than 45,000 Guatemalans disappeared during the war.

The report's focus on Guatemala's inadequate justice system agreed with human rights summaries from other groups including the United Nations Mission for Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala (MINUGUA) and the governmental human rights ombudsman's office.
